governing_thought: The data ecosystem behind Thailand's climate adaptation platform is not yet ready to deliver on its mandate: eleven structural gaps separate what data users need from what the national catalog holds, a distinct combination of these gaps blocks each of the platform's nine planned information services, and 79 percent of the website's required content still needs fresh research or drafting -- together the problem statement this chapter's following sections resolve, starting with the platform's most binding case, A-BTR reporting.

narrative_scqa.situation: DCCE's climate adaptation platform is designed to deliver nine climate information services and a public website drawing on a national dataset catalog, and this chapter opens by establishing how ready that underlying data ecosystem actually is.
narrative_scqa.complication: Comparing what data users actually need against what the catalog and website content currently supply surfaces eleven structural gaps, a distinct combination of which blocks each of the nine planned services, and leaves 79 percent of required website content without a ready source.
narrative_scqa.question: How large and how structured is this shortfall, and what does it mean for developing the platform's services and content?
narrative_scqa.answer: The shortfall is not scattered noise but eleven named structural gaps that combine predictably to block specific services, plus a website content gap concentrated in the 44 percent of required topics that have no source at all -- a problem statement precise enough to act on, which the chapter's following sections, starting with A-BTR in section 4.2, address in turn.

argument_units.claim: Comparing what data users need against what the national catalog supplies separates the shortfall into eleven named structural gaps, not one generic shortage.
argument_units.grounds: WP7 Gap Analysis Report: demand-side interviews, a stakeholder workshop, and a user survey grouped user needs into seven forms -- central reference baselines and indicators, spatial data fine enough to act on, methods for calculating sector impact, access that connects to working systems, a standard way of communicating uncertainty, traceable figures for international climate reporting, and a validated national disaster-loss record. The supply side holds 260 datasets concentrated in six agencies (Thai Meteorological Department 37, DCCE 26, GISTDA 17, Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation 15, National Statistical Office 14, Office of the National Economic and Social Development Council 14), 17% openly published, resolution unrecorded for close to a quarter of entries. Comparing the two produced eleven gaps, each defined in WP7 Section 4 as follows: (1) Balance of hazard/exposure/vulnerability data -- hazard data (climate models, meteorological records, satellite observation) is strong, but data describing the people, assets, and services hazards affect is thinner and more scattered, particularly for infrastructure, economic assets, and social vulnerability. (2) Spatial resolution -- province-level figures support national strategy, but siting decisions (a drain, a seawall height) need sub-district or asset-level grain; the new 5km downscaled climate data closes much of this at the climate-driver end, but the environmental and socio-economic layers needed alongside it are not yet at a matching resolution. (3) Compatibility between spatial units -- hazard data arrives as grids, population/social data as administrative-area boundaries, asset data as points and lines; with no agreed method to relate these, no single resolution can be served reliably. (4) Access -- most of the catalog is available only on request, not published, driven by internal agency sharing rules, personal-data-protection caution, and limited resourcing for automated data connections. (5) Metadata standards -- no agreed national standard yet covers discovery metadata, technical metadata, data dictionaries, or lineage, so a user cannot judge whether a dataset is suitable before relying on it. (6) Product format -- many finished products can only be viewed (e.g. a web map), not downloaded as an analyzable file, which limits their use as an input to further analysis. (7) Time coverage and delay -- different uses need different time horizons (10-20 years of history for baselines, 20-50 years for infrastructure planning, near-real-time for warnings), and the catalog does not yet cover all three consistently. (8) Risk methodology and data selection -- Thailand does not yet have a national approach to defining risk or matching methods to purposes, risking data applied outside the context it was built for. (9) Certification and stewardship -- no step yet exists to check, endorse, and mark a dataset as an official reference (all 260 entries sit in draft status), no dataset has a named steward, and no agreed process exists for when a holding agency declines to share. (10) Calculation methods that do not yet exist -- distinct from Gap 8 (choosing among available methods), several services need a method that has not been built at all: no agreed cost-benefit approach, no standard for classifying climate-related spending, no accepted way to value avoided losses, no damage-function reference library. (11) Decisions awaiting a determination -- several gaps close on a policy or institutional decision rather than on new data or analysis.
argument_units.warrant: Because each gap names a specific, addressable shortfall rather than a vague sense that more data is needed, the platform's next development phase can be planned against a concrete inventory instead of an open-ended research agenda. This precision is what makes the chapter's later recommendations actionable rather than aspirational.
argument_units.application_to_design: The section's opening must state the gap count and, for each of the eleven dimensions, give a brief one-to-two-sentence explanation drawn from its WP7 definition above (not just the name) so the reader understands what each gap actually means, not only that it exists -- while staying at executive altitude (no per-field technical detail).

argument_units.claim: Each of the platform's nine planned information services is blocked by its own distinct combination of the eleven structural gaps, not by data scarcity in general.
argument_units.grounds: WP7 Gap Analysis Report Section 5, "How the Gaps Affect Each Service" -- covers all nine services individually, each with its own gap combination: (1) Certified climate data repository -- no consistent way to classify a dataset as checked/trusted, blocking licensing decisions (Gap 9). (2) High-resolution spatial risk analysis -- the risk index is fixed at province level before calculation and cannot be disaggregated afterward (Gaps 1-3). (3) Finance and budget decision support -- depends on Gap 10 more than any other: no cost-benefit method, spending classification, avoided-loss calculation, or damage-function library exists yet. (4) Historical loss and damage assessment -- relief-spending records are not the same quantity as economic loss; monetary/sectoral breakdown and calculation-manual status remain unresolved (Gaps 1, 3, 7, 10). (5) Engineering design variables -- climate-adjusted design variables (rainfall intensity-duration-frequency, runoff, peak flow) do not exist at any resolution; set aside for the current phase (Gaps 2, 7, 8, 10). (6) Multi-hazard impact-based warning -- the least developed service; no automated connections to sensors, models, or operating agencies exist (Gaps 4, 6, 7). (7) Adaptation policy monitoring and evaluation -- an existing manual platform raises a build-on-or-replace decision, and scattered vulnerability data on differing spatial units limits cross-agency comparison (Gaps 1, 3, 5, 11). (8) Uncertainty management standards -- a methodology/confidence gap, not a data gap: shared institutional understanding of probabilistic projections has not been built (Gaps 5, 8). (9) International climate reporting pipeline -- hand-compiled figures, no shared definitions, poor traceability (Gaps 5, 10); developed in full in section 4.2.
argument_units.warrant: Because different services fail for different structural reasons, a single blanket response such as collecting more data would not unblock most of them. Each service's specific blocking combination has to be named before its development can be sequenced, which is why this section states the obstacle per service rather than a single aggregate count.
argument_units.application_to_design: Present a numbered list naming all nine services with each one's one-line blocking obstacle, per the contract's required structure, not a prose paragraph that blends them together and not a partial/illustrative subset.

argument_units.claim: Against DCCE's 391-item digital asset inventory, only 21 percent (16 of 75) of the website's required content topics are publication-ready, 35 percent (26) are partially populated, and 44 percent (33) have no current source at all -- together 79 percent still needing fresh research or synthesis.
argument_units.grounds: WP4 Content-Source Gap Analysis v2 (2026-08-20): the 75 sitemap-mandated content topics were checked one by one against DCCE's 391-item digital asset inventory, yielding 16 FULL / 26 PARTIAL / 33 GAP.
argument_units.warrant: Because this is a whole-website figure rather than one limited to any single service or reporting obligation, establishing it here corrects an assumption that DCCE already holds most of the content it needs to publish. Placing this baseline in the chapter's front-loaded summary, before any service-specific or A-BTR-specific argument, is why it belongs in this section rather than later.
argument_units.application_to_design: State the three-way split as a short numbered or bulleted breakdown with the 79% headline figure; do not extend into the A-BTR-linked subset of this content gap, which belongs to section 4.2.

argument_units.claim: Because the structural data gaps, the per-service blocking combinations, and the mostly-unready website content describe one interconnected technical problem rather than three separate ones, the chapter's following sections address them in a deliberate order, opening with the platform's most binding case, A-BTR reporting.
argument_units.grounds: WP7 Gap Analysis Report's own structure: it moves from demand/supply gaps through per-service blockers to the same eleven-gap inventory recurring across every service and the content shortfall, showing the three findings are facets of one technical shortfall rather than independent problems. (Note: WP7's institutional-gap synthesis -- the absence of a coordinating role across agencies -- is deliberately not used here; that argument belongs to section 4.4, which owns the institutional/governance conclusion. Section 4.1 stays scoped to the technical gap inventory only.)
argument_units.warrant: Because A-BTR is a binding, recurring international reporting obligation rather than a discretionary service, and because it draws on several of the same structural gaps and the same content-readiness shortfall just established, developing it first in section 4.2 grounds the chapter's remaining recommendations in the sharpest version of the technical problem rather than an averaged one.
argument_units.application_to_design: Close this section with a brief transition naming A-BTR as the next section's focus, without developing the A-BTR argument itself here.
